text:
You need about **300 to 400 W of solar** to refill a 1000Wh power station in one good sunny day. For a slower recharge over 2 days, 200 W is enough.

**The formula** (from [Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge)): panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.75 = Wh per day. The 0.75 covers real-world losses from heat, angle, wiring and charge controller inefficiency.

Rearranged, panel watts needed = 1000 ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.75).

| Peak sun hours | Panel for a 1-day recharge | Panel for a 2-day recharge |
|---|---|---|
| 3 hrs (cloudy, winter, north) | ~445 W | ~220 W |
| 4 hrs (typical) | ~335 W | ~170 W |
| 5 hrs (sunny) | ~270 W | ~135 W |
| 6 hrs (desert, summer) | ~225 W | ~110 W |

**Practical tips**
- **Check the station's solar input limit.** Many 1000Wh units accept only 200 to 600 W of solar. A bigger panel array than that won't charge it faster.
- **Check voltage and current limits.** Panels wired in series or parallel must fit the station's voltage and amp range.
- **Real output is lower than the label.** Flat placement, partial shade, haze and heat can cut output well below the rated watts. Angle the panels toward the sun and adjust them during the day.
- **Plan for a bit of margin.** For most people, a 400 W setup (or 2×200 W) is a good match for a 1000Wh station. It recharges in about 1 day in good sun and still works reasonably on weaker days.

Sources: [Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge). I didn't open the other results, so the table and tips come from this formula and general knowledge.
